title: Statistics: descriptive and spread; Statistical tests; Factors affecting enzyme activity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR03a#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR03b#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR02b#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR03a#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ02#N.3a, PR02b#N.7a, PR03a#N.3, PR03b#N.7, EZ02#N.6a, PR03a#N.11, PR03b#N.9, EZ02#N.8a, EZ02#N.11a, EZ02#N.14a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Degrees of freedom
items.clue: Number of categories minus 1 in a χ² calculation.

items.label: Null hypothesis
items.clue: States that there is no significant difference between the two means.

items.label: Range
items.clue: Runs from the minimum to the maximum, so it depends on only two values.

items.label: Critical value
items.clue: Cut-off at p = 0.05 above which a calculated result counts as significant.

questions.stem: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³ (illustrative data). What is the best estimate of the initial rate of reaction from these data?

options.text: 0.4 cm³ s⁻¹
20 seconds
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹. With readings every 20 s, this first-interval rate is the best estimate the data allow.

questions.stem: A student grew bean seedlings with fertiliser X or fertiliser Y, 10 plants each. Mean root length ± 1 standard deviation: X, 42 mm (bar from 33 to 51 mm); Y, 47 mm (bar from 39 to 55 mm). Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Fertiliser Y gave significantly longer roots, because its mean is 5 mm higher.
Every root grown with fertiliser X was between 33 and 51 mm long.
The SD bars overlap widely, so the difference may be due to chance alone.
The SD bars overlap, which proves that the two fertilisers have exactly the same effect.

questions.explanation: Most of each bar lies within the other. Many plants in the two groups had similar roots. A t-test, using sample size, would decide whether 5 mm is significant.

questions.stem: A student measures the lengths of 20 leaves from plants growing in the sun and 20 from plants growing in the shade. She wants to know whether mean leaf length differs between the two. Which statistical test should she use?

options.text: Chi-squared, because she is comparing two groups of plants.
Student's t-test, because she is comparing the means of two sets of continuous data.
A correlation coefficient, because she wants to know whether light is related to leaf length.
No test is needed: if the two means differ, the difference is real.

questions.explanation: Two groups, one measured variable, a difference in means: that is what the t-test is for.

questions.stem: For 10 quadrats, a student ranks the density of a moss and the soil moisture content, and finds Σd² = 60. The critical value of rₛ for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: rₛ = 0.64, which is below 0.648, so there is no significant correlation.
rₛ = 0.36, a weak positive correlation that is not significant.
rₛ = 0.64, a positive value, so there is a significant positive correlation.
rₛ = 0.64, which is greater than 0.05, so the correlation is significant.

questions.explanation: rₛ = 1 − (6 × 60) ÷ (10 × 99) = 1 − 360 ÷ 990 = 0.64. Just below the critical value: the correlation could be due to chance.

questions.stem: A student measured the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at six temperatures. The rates, in arbitrary units, were: 10 °C, 2; 20 °C, 4; 30 °C, 8; 40 °C, 15; 50 °C, 9; 60 °C, 1 (illustrative data). Which conclusion is supported by these data?

options.text: The low rate at 10 °C shows that the enzyme had been denatured by the cold temperature.
The true optimum is 37 °C, the body temperature at which every enzyme works at its best.
The optimum is near 40 °C; above it, denaturation outweighs the faster collisions.
The fall in rate after 40 °C shows that the substrate had been used up at higher temperatures.

questions.stem: A 1999 study found that children who had slept with a light on before the age of two were more likely to become short-sighted later. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on at night, and short sight is partly inherited. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Night-time lighting causes short sight, because the 1999 correlation was found in a large group of children.
The correlation can be explained by parents' short sight, which is linked to both variables.
The 1999 correlation must have been a mistake: the children with night lights were not really more short-sighted.
The later studies prove that light at night has no effect on the eye at all.

questions.stem: A student counts the heart rate of Daphnia in pond water (control) and in a caffeine solution, 10 Daphnia in each. - Control: mean 212 beats per minute, SD 18. - Caffeine: mean 231 beats per minute, SD 20. Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 9 degrees of freedom, 2.26; 18, 2.10; 20, 2.09. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: t = 9.75, far above 2.10, so the difference is highly significant.
t = 2.23, above 2.10 for 18 degrees of freedom, so reject the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, below 2.26 for 9 degrees of freedom, so accept the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, above 2.10, which proves caffeine raises the heart rate of every Daphnia.

questions.stem: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. When it passes with food into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity falls almost to zero. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The change in pH alters charges on amino acids, disrupting bonds that hold the active site's shape.
The alkaline conditions hydrolyse the peptide bonds of pepsin, breaking it up into free amino acids.
Pepsin has run out of substrate, because protein digestion is completed inside the stomach.
At pH 8 the enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly, so they collide less often.

questions.stem: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?

options.text: The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.

questions.explanation: At saturation, as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.

questions.stem: An enzyme from a cold-water fish has an optimum temperature of about 15 °C. A sample was kept at 45 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled back to 15 °C. Its activity at 15 °C was only 5% of that of an unheated sample tested at the same time (illustrative data). Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The heat killed the enzyme molecules, so they no longer worked at 15 °C.
Heat broke bonds holding its shape; the active site changed and did not re-form.
At 15 °C the molecules moved too slowly to collide, so activity was low.
The heat broke its peptide bonds, splitting the enzyme into separate amino acids.

questions.explanation: At 45 °C hydrogen and ionic bonds broke and the active site lost its complementary shape. Cooling did not restore it: the enzyme was denatured.
